subproblem.title: Piece-counting functions increase pointwise to the multiplicity fiberCount (Simon 2.1.8(ii), counting step)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X Y : Type) [MetricSpace X] (A : Set X) (f : X → Y) (P : ℕ → ℕ → Set X), (∀ i j k, j ≠ k → Disjoint (P i j) (P i k)) → (∀ i, ⋃ j, P i j = Set.univ) → (∀ i j, ∀ x ∈ P i j, ∀ x' ∈ P i j, dist x x' < 1 / ((i : ℝ) + 1)) → (∀ i j, ∃ k, P (i + 1) j ⊆ P i k) → ∀ y : Y, Monotone (fun i ↦ ∑' j, (f '' (A ∩ P i j)).indicator (1 : Y → ℝ≥0∞) y) ∧ ⨆ i, ∑' j, (f '' (A ∩ P i j)).indicator (1 : Y → ℝ≥0∞) y = fiberCount A f y
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 2, Theorem 1.8(ii), printed proof (p. 45). No erratum.

Printed text: 'Observe that then Σ_j χ_{f(A_ij)} is a non-negative function … which increases pointwise (at every point) to N(f, y)'. Here N(f,y) = H⁰(A ∩ f⁻¹y) = fiberCount A f y = encard(A ∩ f⁻¹{y}) ∈ [0,∞] and A_ij := A ∩ P i j. The detailed argument is Part II step 7(a)-(c) of the parent proof.

Fix y ∈ Y. Cardinalities are Set.encard ∈ ℕ∞, cast to [0,∞] by ENat.toENNReal (monotone, with ENat.toENNReal_le).

1. Empty space. If X is empty, then A = ∅ and every f(A ∩ P i j) = ∅. So every N_i(y) = 0, the constant sequence 0 is monotone with supremum 0, and fiberCount ∅ f y = encard ∅ = 0. Assume now that X is nonempty; this only makes the choice functions below total.
2. Counting functions are cardinalities. Put J_i := {j ∈ ℕ : y ∈ f(A ∩ P i j)} and S := A ∩ f⁻¹{y}, so fiberCount A f y = encard S by definition. The j-th summand 1_{f(A ∩ P i j)}(y) is 1 if j ∈ J_i and 0 otherwise, i.e. it is the value at j of the indicator of J_i with value 1. Hence N_i(y) = Σ'_{j ∈ J_i} 1 = encard J_i (tsum_subtype and ENNReal.tsum_set_one); this is ∞ when J_i is infinite.
3. Unique pieces. Since ∪_j P i j = X, every x ∈ X lies in some P i j. By pairwise disjointness, if x ∈ P i j and x ∈ P i k then j = k.
4. Bound (b): encard J_i ≤ encard S. For each j ∈ J_i choose x_j ∈ A ∩ P i j with f(x_j) = y. Then x_j ∈ S. The map j ↦ x_j is injective on J_i: if x_j = x_k, this point lies in P i j and in P i k, so j = k by step 3. An injection J_i → S gives encard J_i ≤ encard S (Set.encard_le_encard_of_injOn).
5. Monotonicity (a): encard J_i ≤ encard J_{i+1}. With x_j as in step 4, let p(j) be an index with x_j ∈ P (i+1) p(j) (step 3). Since x_j ∈ A and f(x_j) = y, p(j) ∈ J_{i+1}. The map p is injective on J_i: if p(j) = p(k) =: c, the nesting hypothesis gives k′ with P (i+1) c ⊆ P i k′; then x_j ∈ P i j ∩ P i k′ and x_k ∈ P i k ∩ P i k′, so j = k′ = k by step 3. Hence encard J_i ≤ encard J_{i+1}. By step 2 and monotonicity of the cast, N_i(y) ≤ N_{i+1}(y) for all i, so i ↦ N_i(y) is monotone (monotone_nat_of_le_succ).
6. Exhaustion (c): for every natural number n with n ≤ encard S there is i with n ≤ encard J_i.
 - Given such n, choose F ⊆ S with encard F = n (Set.exists_subset_encard_eq); F is finite.
 - For each of the finitely many pairs (x, x′) ∈ F × F with x ≠ x′, dist(x, x′) > 0 and 1/(i+1) → 0, so 1/(i+1) < dist(x, x′) for all sufficiently large i. Since there are finitely many pairs, one i works for all of them: 1/(i+1) < dist(x, x′) for all distinct x, x′ ∈ F (Filter.eventually_all_finset, tendsto_one_div_add_atTop_nhds_zero_nat).
 - For x ∈ F let p(x) be the index with x ∈ P i p(x) (step 3). As x ∈ A and f(x) = y, p(x) ∈ J_i.
 - p is injective on F: if x ≠ x′ and p(x) = p(x′), then x, x′ ∈ P i p(x), so dist(x, x′) < 1/(i+1) by the mesh hypothesis, contradicting the choice of i.
 - Therefore n = encard F ≤ encard J_i.
7. Conclusion. By steps 2 and 4, N_i(y) ≤ fiberCount A f y for every i, so sup_i N_i(y) ≤ fiberCount A f y. For the reverse inequality:
 - If encard S = k ∈ ℕ, step 6 with n = k gives i with k ≤ encard J_i, so fiberCount A f y = k ≤ N_i(y) ≤ sup_i N_i(y).
 - If encard S = ∞, then for every real r ≥ 0 pick a natural n > r (ENNReal.exists_nat_gt). Step 6 gives i with n ≤ encard J_i, so r < n ≤ N_i(y) ≤ sup_i N_i(y). Hence sup_i N_i(y) = ∞ = fiberCount A f y (ENNReal.eq_top_of_forall_nnreal_le).
 So sup_i N_i(y) = fiberCount A f y. Together with step 5, both conjuncts hold for the arbitrary fixed y.
proof_key_steps: Empty X is trivial; otherwise N_i(y) = encard J_i with J_i = {j : y ∈ f(A ∩ P i j)} (tsum_subtype, ENNReal.tsum_set_one), and fiberCount A f y = encard S, S = A ∩ f⁻¹{y}.
Each point lies in exactly one P i j (cover + disjointness).
encard J_i ≤ encard S via the injection j ↦ chosen point of A ∩ P i j ∩ f⁻¹{y}.
encard J_i ≤ encard J_{i+1} via j ↦ the level-(i+1) piece containing that point, which is injective by nesting + disjointness; hence monotone.
For a finite F ⊆ S of size n, a level i with 1/(i+1) below all distances in F separates F into distinct pieces, so n ≤ encard J_i; hence sup_i N_i(y) = fiberCount A f y (finite and infinite cases).

audit.reason: The exact type matches both claimed conclusions and all partition hypotheses. Indicator sums equal coerced encard values. The two explicit injections prove the upper bound and monotonicity. Separation of arbitrary finite fiber subsets proves the reverse supremum inequality, including infinite and uncountable fibers. Empty cases and cardinality coercions are handled; no measurability assumptions or parent theorem are used.

subproblem.title: Simon-normalized Hausdorff measure of a Lipschitz image (Simon 2.1.8(i), inequality)
subproblem.statement: Let X and Y be metric spaces with their Borel σ-algebras, m ≥ 0 a real number, and 𝓗^m := Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m = (ω_m/2^m)·μH[m] (on X and on Y). Let E ⊆ X be an arbitrary set (no measurability assumed), K ∈ ℝ≥0, and f : X → Y K-Lipschitz on E (LipschitzOnWith K f E). Then 𝓗^m(f(E)) ≤ K^m·𝓗^m(E) in [0,∞], where K^m is the extended-real power (ENNReal.rpow).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X Y : Type) [MetricSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [BorelSpace X] [MetricSpace Y] [MeasurableSpace Y] [BorelSpace Y] (m : ℝ) (E : Set X) (f : X → Y) (K : ℝ≥0), 0 ≤ m → LipschitzOnWith K f E → Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m (f '' E) ≤ (K : ℝ≥0∞) ^ m * Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m E
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 2, Theorem 1.8(i), first paragraph of the printed proof (pp. 44-45). No erratum.

Printed text: 'Observe first that if δ > 0 and if C₁, C₂, … are chosen with A ⊆ ∪_j C_j and diam C_j < δ for each j, then f(A) ⊆ ∪_j f(C_j) and diam(f(C_j)) ≤ (Lip f)δ < (1 + Lip f)δ. Hence H^m_{(1+Lip f)δ}(f(A)) ≤ Σ_j ω_m (diam f(C_j)/2)^m ≤ (Lip f)^m Σ_j ω_m (diam C_j/2)^m, and taking inf over all such collections {C_j} and then letting δ ↓ 0 we obtain H^m(f(A)) ≤ (Lip f)^m H^m(A). Notice this part of the argument is valid even if A is not H^m-measurable and did not depend on the σ-compactness of X.'

Conventions: the set is an arbitrary E ⊆ X; f : X → Y is only assumed K-Lipschitz on E; K plays the role of Lip f; and 𝓗^m := Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m = c_m • μH[m] with c_m := realUnitBallVolume m / 2^m = ω_m/2^m ∈ [0,∞].

1. Covering argument for μH[m]. Let δ > 0 and let C₁, C₂, … be sets with E ⊆ ∪_j C_j and diam C_j < δ. Put C′_j := E ∩ C_j. Then f(E) = ∪_j f(C′_j). Since f is K-Lipschitz on E ⊇ C′_j, diam f(C′_j) ≤ K·diam C′_j ≤ K·diam C_j ≤ Kδ < (1+K)δ. Hence the size-(1+K)δ approximating sum of f(E) is at most Σ_j (diam f(C′_j))^m ≤ K^m·Σ_j (diam C_j)^m. Taking the infimum over all such covers and letting δ ↓ 0 gives μH[m](f(E)) ≤ K^m·μH[m](E). This is precisely Mathlib's LipschitzOnWith.hausdorffMeasure_image_le applied to h : LipschitzOnWith K f E and hd : 0 ≤ m, which yields μH[m] (f '' E) ≤ (K : ℝ≥0∞)^m * μH[m] E. It holds for every set E, every m ≥ 0 (including m = 0) and every K ≥ 0.
2. Normalization. By the definition of Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal, 𝓗^m = c_m • μH[m] as measures on X and on Y. So 𝓗^m(S) = c_m·μH[m](S) for every set S (Measure.smul_apply and smul_eq_mul in ℝ≥0∞).
3. Scaling. Multiplication by the fixed element c_m of [0,∞] is monotone, so step 1 gives 𝓗^m(f(E)) = c_m·μH[m](f(E)) ≤ c_m·(K^m·μH[m](E)).
4. Rearranging. Multiplication in [0,∞] is commutative and associative (mul_left_comm), so c_m·(K^m·μH[m](E)) = K^m·(c_m·μH[m](E)), which equals K^m·𝓗^m(E) by step 2.
5. Combining steps 3 and 4 gives 𝓗^m(f(E)) ≤ K^m·𝓗^m(E), which is the claim. No measurability of E and no σ-compactness was used.
proof_key_steps: Covering argument: μH[m](f(E)) ≤ K^m·μH[m](E) for any E on which f is K-Lipschitz (Mathlib LipschitzOnWith.hausdorffMeasure_image_le, needs 0 ≤ m).
Multiply by the constant ω_m/2^m and reassociate (mul_left_comm) to get 𝓗^m(f(E)) ≤ K^m·𝓗^m(E).

audit.reason: The prose and exact Lean proposition match. Restricting covers to E respects the Lipschitz-on hypothesis. The pinned Hausdorff-image lemma includes m = 0 and K = 0; multiplication by the common normalization factor proves the stated bound. No measurability, sigma-compactness, or circular reliance is introduced.

subproblem.title: Nested countable Borel partitions of a separable metric space with mesh 1/(i+1)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type) [MetricSpace X] [TopologicalSpace.SeparableSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [BorelSpace X], ∃ P : ℕ → ℕ → Set X, (∀ i j, MeasurableSet (P i j)) ∧ (∀ i j k, j ≠ k → Disjoint (P i j) (P i k)) ∧ (∀ i, ⋃ j, P i j = Set.univ) ∧ (∀ i j, ∀ x ∈ P i j, ∀ x' ∈ P i j, dist x x' < 1 / ((i : ℝ) + 1)) ∧ (∀ i j, ∃ k, P (i + 1) j ⊆ P i k)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 2, Theorem 1.8(ii), printed proof (p. 45). No erratum.

Printed text: 'by the σ-compactness of X, for each i = 1, 2, … we can partition A into a disjoint union ∪_{j=1}^∞ A_{ij} where each A_{ij} is H^m-measurable and diam(A_{ij}) < 1/i; furthermore we can do this successively, partitioning each A_{ik} to give the new sets A_{i+1,j}, so that each of the sets A_{i+1,j} is contained in one of the A_{ik}.'

As in Part II step 5 of the parent proof, all of X is partitioned into Borel sets (Simon's A_{ij} are then A ∩ P i j). σ-compactness enters only through separability (a σ-compact metric space is separable), which is the hypothesis here. Indices start at i = 0 with mesh 1/(i+1). 'diam < 1/(i+1)' is stated as 'any two points are at distance < 1/(i+1)'. Empty pieces are allowed.

1. Empty space. If X is empty, set P i j := ∅ for all i, j. Each ∅ is Borel, any two are disjoint, ∪_j P i j = ∅ = X, the distance condition is vacuous, and P (i+1) j = ∅ ⊆ P i 0. Assume from now on that X is nonempty.
2. Dense sequence. X is a nonempty separable space, so there is q : ℕ → X with dense range (Mathlib TopologicalSpace.exists_dense_seq). In a metric space this means: for every x ∈ X and r > 0 there is l with dist(x, q_l) < r (DenseRange.exists_dist_lt).
3. One level. For i ∈ ℕ let r_i := 1/(3(i+1)) > 0 and Q_{i,l} := B(q_l, r_i) ∖ ∪_{l′<l} B(q_{l′}, r_i), with B the open ball. This is Mathlib's disjointed (fun l ↦ ball (q l) (r_i)) l. Properties:
 (a) Q_{i,l} is Borel, as a finite Boolean combination of open balls (MeasurableSet.disjointed, measurableSet_ball).
 (b) Q_{i,l} ∩ Q_{i,l′} = ∅ for l ≠ l′: if l′ < l, then Q_{i,l} is disjoint from B(q_{l′}, r_i) ⊇ Q_{i,l′} (disjoint_disjointed).
 (c) ∪_l Q_{i,l} = ∪_l B(q_l, r_i) = X (iUnion_disjointed). By step 2 every x has some l with dist(x, q_l) < r_i, and x ∈ Q_{i,l} for the least such l.
 (d) Q_{i,l} ⊆ B(q_l, r_i) (disjointed_subset).
4. Refinement by recursion. Let (u(n), v(n)) := Nat.unpair n, so Nat.unpair (Nat.pair a b) = (a, b) and Nat.pair (u(n)) (v(n)) = n (Nat.unpair_pair, Nat.pair_unpair). Define P 0 n := Q_{0,n} and P (i+1) n := P i (u(n)) ∩ Q_{i+1, v(n)}. The members of the i-th family are then exactly the intersections Q_{0,l₀} ∩ … ∩ Q_{i,l_i}, as in the parent proof, re-indexed by ℕ.
5. Borel (property 1), by induction on i. P 0 n = Q_{0,n} is Borel by 3(a). P (i+1) n is the intersection of the Borel sets P i (u(n)) (induction hypothesis) and Q_{i+1,v(n)}.
6. Disjoint (property 2), by induction on i. For i = 0 this is 3(b). For i+1, let n ≠ n′. Then (u(n), v(n)) ≠ (u(n′), v(n′)), because n = pair(u(n), v(n)) and n′ = pair(u(n′), v(n′)).
 - If u(n) ≠ u(n′), then P i (u(n)) and P i (u(n′)) are disjoint by the induction hypothesis, hence so are their subsets P (i+1) n and P (i+1) n′.
 - Otherwise v(n) ≠ v(n′), and P (i+1) n ⊆ Q_{i+1,v(n)} and P (i+1) n′ ⊆ Q_{i+1,v(n′)} are disjoint by 3(b).
7. Cover (property 3), by induction on i. For i = 0 this is 3(c). For i+1, let x ∈ X. By the induction hypothesis x ∈ P i j for some j, and by 3(c) x ∈ Q_{i+1,l} for some l. For n := Nat.pair j l we have (u(n), v(n)) = (j, l), so x ∈ P i j ∩ Q_{i+1,l} = P (i+1) n. Hence ∪_n P (i+1) n = X.
8. Mesh (property 4). For every i and n there is l with P i n ⊆ Q_{i,l}: take l = n if i = 0, and l = v(n) if i = i′+1 (since P (i′+1) n ⊆ Q_{i′+1,v(n)}). So for x, x′ ∈ P i n, 3(d) gives dist(x, q_l) < r_i and dist(x′, q_l) < r_i. Therefore dist(x, x′) ≤ dist(x, q_l) + dist(x′, q_l) < 2r_i = (2/3)·1/(i+1) < 1/(i+1).
9. Nested (property 5). For all i, n: P (i+1) n = P i (u(n)) ∩ Q_{i+1,v(n)} ⊆ P i (u(n)), so take k := u(n).
10. Steps 5-9 establish properties (1)-(5) for P (and step 1 covers empty X), which proves the theorem.
proof_key_steps: Empty X: take all pieces empty.
Dense sequence q (exists_dense_seq); level-i sets Q_{i,l} := disjointed open balls B(q_l, 1/(3(i+1))), which are Borel, disjoint, cover X, and lie in a ball.
Recursive refinement P 0 n := Q_{0,n}, P (i+1) n := P i (unpair n).1 ∩ Q_{i+1,(unpair n).2}.
Measurability, disjointness and covering by induction on i, using Nat.pair/Nat.unpair being inverse bijections.
Mesh: each P i n lies in a ball of radius 1/(3(i+1)), so distances are < 2/(3(i+1)) < 1/(i+1); nesting P (i+1) n ⊆ P i (unpair n).1.

audit.reason: The statement and Lean type agree, including allowance for empty pieces. The proof handles empty X, constructs disjoint Borel ball pieces from a dense sequence, and recursively refines them using Nat.pair/unpair. The induction verifies covering, disjointness, measurability, strict mesh bounds, and refinement without additional hypotheses.

subproblem.title: Null-measurability of Lipschitz images under Simon-normalized Hausdorff measure (Simon 2.1.8(i), measurability)
subproblem.statement: Let X be a σ-compact metric space and Y a metric space, both with their Borel σ-algebras. Let m ≥ 0 be real and 𝓗^m := Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m (on X and on Y). Let A ⊆ X be 𝓗^m-null-measurable with 𝓗^m(A) < ∞, K ∈ ℝ≥0, and f : X → Y K-Lipschitz on A. Then f(A) is 𝓗^m-null-measurable in Y.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X Y : Type) [MetricSpace X] [SigmaCompactSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] [BorelSpace X] [MetricSpace Y] [MeasurableSpace Y] [BorelSpace Y] (m : ℝ) (A : Set X) (f : X → Y) (K : ℝ≥0), 0 ≤ m → NullMeasurableSet A (Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m) → Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m A < ⊤ → LipschitzOnWith K f A → NullMeasurableSet (f '' A) (Chapter01.simonHausdorffMeasureReal m)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 2, Theorem 1.8(i), second paragraph of the printed proof (p. 45). No erratum.

Printed text: 'Next suppose that A is H^m-measurable and observe that the regularity property 1.15(2) of Ch. 1 together with the σ-compactness of X implies that we can take a sequence K₁, K₂, … of compact sets in X with K_j ⊆ A for each j and H^m(A∖(∪_j K_j)) = 0. By the first part above we then have H^m(f(A∖(∪_j K_j))) = 0 and hence f(A) = f(A∖(∪_j K_j)) ∪ (∪_j f(K_j)). Now f(K_j) is compact, hence Borel, for each j, and H^m(f(A∖(∪_j K_j))) ≤ (Lip f)^m H^m(A∖(∪_j K_j)) = 0, so f(A) is H^m-measurable as claimed.'

Conventions: Carathéodory 𝓗^m-measurability is rendered as NullMeasurableSet for the Borel measure μ := 𝓗^m (on X and on Y). The 'first part' is the sibling theorem image_measure_le.

1. Null sets have null images. Let E ⊆ A with μ(E) = 0. Then f is K-Lipschitz on E (restriction of LipschitzOnWith K f A). By image_measure_le with this E (using 0 ≤ m), μ(f(E)) ≤ K^m·μ(E) = K^m·0 = 0, so μ(f(E)) = 0.
2. Borel kernel of A. A is μ-null-measurable, so there is a Borel set B ⊆ A with B = A μ-a.e. (Mathlib NullMeasurableSet.exists_measurable_subset_ae_eq). In particular μ(A ∖ B) = 0 (ae_le_set), and μ(B) ≤ μ(A) < ∞.
3. Compact sets inside B (Simon's appeal to 1.15(2) and σ-compactness). Let ν := μ.restrict B. Then ν(X) = μ(B) < ∞, so ν is a finite, hence locally finite, Borel measure on the σ-compact metric space X. A locally finite Borel measure on a σ-compact pseudometrizable space is regular (Mathlib instance Measure.Regular.of_sigmaCompactSpace_of_isLocallyFiniteMeasure). It is therefore inner regular by compact sets on Borel sets of finite measure, and Mathlib MeasurableSet.exists_isCompact_sdiff_lt applies (X is Hausdorff with its Borel σ-algebra). For each j ∈ ℕ, apply it to the Borel set B (ν(B) = μ(B) < ∞) with ε = (j : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹ ≠ 0 (for j = 0 this is ∞). This gives a compact C_j ⊆ B with ν(B ∖ C_j) < 1/j.
4. The uncovered part of A is null. Put D := A ∖ ∪_j C_j, so D ⊆ A.
 - B ∖ ∪_j C_j is Borel (compact sets are closed, hence Borel) and contained in B. So μ(B ∖ ∪_j C_j) = ν(B ∖ ∪_j C_j) ≤ ν(B ∖ C_j) < 1/j for every j. Since 1/j → 0, μ(B ∖ ∪_j C_j) = 0.
 - Each x ∈ D lies in A ∖ B (if x ∉ B) or in B ∖ ∪_j C_j (if x ∈ B). So D ⊆ (A ∖ B) ∪ (B ∖ ∪_j C_j), hence μ(D) ≤ 0 + 0, i.e. μ(D) = 0.
 These C_j are Simon's K_j, with H^m(A ∖ ∪_j K_j) = 0.
5. Borel part of the image. For each j, C_j ⊆ B ⊆ A, so f is K-Lipschitz, hence continuous, on C_j. Thus f(C_j) is compact, hence closed in the metric space Y, hence Borel. Therefore G := ∪_j f(C_j) is a Borel subset of Y with G ⊆ f(A).
6. The rest of the image is null. Let y ∈ f(A) ∖ G and write y = f(x) with x ∈ A. If x were in some C_j, then y ∈ f(C_j) ⊆ G; so x ∉ ∪_j C_j and x ∈ D. Hence f(A) ∖ G ⊆ f(D). By steps 1 and 4 (D ⊆ A, μ(D) = 0), μ(f(A) ∖ G) ≤ μ(f(D)) = 0.
7. Conclusion. Since G ⊆ f(A), f(A) = G ∪ (f(A) ∖ G) (Set.union_diff_cancel). G is Borel, hence μ-null-measurable. f(A) ∖ G is μ-null, hence μ-null-measurable (NullMeasurableSet.of_null). A finite union of null-measurable sets is null-measurable, so f(A) is μ-null-measurable. (This is the argument of SimonGMT Chapter02.nullMeasurableSet_image_of_lipschitzOn_sigmaCompact(_of_nullMeasurable), transferred from μHE[n] to 𝓗^m with real m ≥ 0.)
proof_key_steps: Null subsets E ⊆ A have null images, by image_measure_le.
Borel kernel B ⊆ A with μ(A∖B) = 0 (NullMeasurableSet.exists_measurable_subset_ae_eq).
μ.restrict B is finite on a σ-compact metric space, hence regular: compact C_j ⊆ B with μ(B∖C_j) < 1/j (MeasurableSet.exists_isCompact_sdiff_lt).
f(A) = (∪_j f(C_j)) ∪ (f(A) ∖ ∪_j f(C_j)): a Borel set (compact images) union a subset of the null set f(D), hence null-measurable.

audit.reason: All hypotheses are explicit and used correctly. The measurable kernel has finite measure, so its restricted measure is regular on the sigma-compact metric domain. Compact approximation leaves a null residual; the declared image_measure_le dependency makes its image null. Compact images supply the Borel part. This proves exactly the requested null-measurability.
